title: 1 Kings 22:29–40
context: Ahab disguises himself for the battle while Jehoshaphat wears his royal robes; the Syrian captains pursue Jehoshaphat until they realize he is not the king of Israel. A bow drawn at random strikes Ahab between the joints of his armor, and he dies at evening; the dogs lick his blood when his chariot is washed by the pool of Samaria, “according to the LORD’s word which he spoke.” Both traditions read this as shared ground on God’s word being fulfilled, Verse 21:19 had spoken of dogs licking Ahab’s blood in the place where they licked Naboth’s, while 22:38 records this at the pool of Samaria; interpreters discuss how the details correspond and do not agree on one account.

verses.text: So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So the king of Israel and Jehoshaphat the king of Judah went up to Ramoth Gilead.” Arminian readers note that both kings go ahead despite Micaiah’s clear warning.

Jehoshaphat, who asked for the LORD’s word, does not act on it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see both kings walking into the judgment that was announced.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: hearing God’s word and still going one’s own way is a danger for the faithful as well as for the faithless.

verses.text: The king of Israel said to Jehoshaphat, “I will disguise myself and go into the battle, but you put on your robes.” The king of Israel disguised himself and went into the battle.
verses.arminianNotes:
Ahab says, “I will disguise myself and go into the battle, but you put on your robes.” Arminian readers note that he tries to evade the word while leaving his ally exposed.

The disguise shows he took the prophecy more seriously than he admitted.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a futile attempt to escape God’s decree.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: human schemes cannot overturn what the LORD has spoken.

verses.text: Now the king of Syria had commanded the thirty-two captains of his chariots, saying, “Don’t fight with small nor great, except only with the king of Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The king of Syria commands his thirty-two captains to fight only with the king of Israel. Arminian readers note that the order targets Ahab, perhaps recalling his earlier dealings with Ben Hadad (20:34), though the text gives no motive.

The command sets up the danger to Jehoshaphat.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the scene arranged so that Ahab’s fate will be clear.

Both traditions note that the order leaves Jehoshaphat, still in his royal robes, exposed to the danger meant for Ahab.

verses.text: When the captains of the chariots saw Jehoshaphat, they said, “Surely that is the king of Israel!” and they came over to fight against him. Jehoshaphat cried out.
verses.arminianNotes:
The captains see Jehoshaphat, think he is the king of Israel, and turn to fight him, and “Jehoshaphat cried out.” Arminian readers note the danger his alliance has brought him.

2 Chronicles 18:31 adds that the LORD helped him and drew them away.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s protection of Jehoshaphat even when he has walked into danger by his own choice.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: God can rescue his people from the consequences of an unwise decision, though they should not presume on it.

verses.text: When the captains of the chariots saw that it was not the king of Israel, they turned back from pursuing him.
verses.arminianNotes:
When the captains see that he is not the king of Israel, they turn back. Arminian readers note Jehoshaphat’s deliverance as an act of mercy.

The disguise meant to protect Ahab nearly cost Jehoshaphat his life.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the LORD’s preserving care for the king of Judah.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: God is merciful to his servant in a moment of danger.

verses.text: A certain man drew his bow at random, and struck the king of Israel between the joints of the armor. Therefore he said to the driver of his chariot, “Turn around, and carry me out of the battle, for I am severely wounded.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“A certain man drew his bow at random, and struck the king of Israel between the joints of the armor.” Arminian readers note that the archer acts freely and without aim, yet the word of the LORD is fulfilled.

God’s purposes are accomplished through ordinary human actions.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see providence guiding even an arrow shot at random (cf. Prov 16:33).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the disguise could not hide Ahab from the LORD’s word, though they describe how God governs such events in different terms.

verses.text: The battle increased that day. The king was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians, and died at evening. The blood ran out of the wound into the bottom of the chariot.
verses.arminianNotes:
The battle increases, the king is propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians, and he dies at evening. Arminian readers note the sober detail of his death.

He dies facing the enemy, as the prophecy foretold.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the fulfillment of Micaiah’s word that the king would not return in peace (22:28).

Both traditions read the death soberly as God’s judgment, not with triumph.

verses.text: A cry went throughout the army about the going down of the sun, saying, “Every man to his city, and every man to his country!”
verses.arminianNotes:
A cry goes through the army at sunset: “Every man to his city, and every man to his country!” Arminian readers note that this fulfills Micaiah’s vision of Israel scattered without a shepherd (22:17).

The army disperses, as was foretold.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the precision of God’s word in the scattering of the army.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the LORD’s word through Micaiah came true in every detail he spoke.

verses.text: So the king died, and was brought to Samaria; and they buried the king in Samaria.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So the king died, and was brought to Samaria; and they buried the king in Samaria.” Arminian readers note that the king who promised to return in peace returns dead.

The narrator states the outcome plainly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see Micaiah’s prophecy fulfilled in the king’s death.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Ahab’s death confirms that the LORD had spoken through Micaiah (22:28).

verses.text: They washed the chariot by the pool of Samaria; and the dogs licked up his blood where the prostitutes washed themselves, according to the LORD’s word which he spoke.
verses.arminianNotes:
Of Ahab’s blood the text says, “the dogs licked up his blood where the prostitutes washed themselves, according to the LORD’s word which he spoke.” Arminian readers note that the narrator links this to the word against Ahab (21:19).

21:19 speaks of “the place where dogs licked the blood of Naboth,” which was at Jezreel, while 22:38 is at the pool of Samaria.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also see the fulfillment of the LORD’s word.

Interpreters discuss how 22:38 relates to 21:19, to 21:29 (“I will not bring the evil in his days”), and to 2 Kings 9:25–26; both traditions note this as an open issue.

verses.text: Now the rest of the acts of Ahab, and all that he did, and the ivory house which he built, and all the cities that he built, aren’t they written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel?
verses.arminianNotes:
The rest of Ahab’s acts, including “the ivory house which he built,” are written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel. Arminian readers note that Ahab’s building achievements are acknowledged.

The narrator’s interest lies in his response to God’s word.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the contrast between Ahab’s outward success and his spiritual failure (cf. Amos 3:15).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: prosperity and achievement do not measure faithfulness.

verses.text: So Ahab slept with his fathers; and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So Ahab slept with his fathers; and Ahaziah his son reigned in his place.” Arminian readers note the standard formula, used even though Ahab died in battle.

The kingdom continues under his son.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the transition to Ahaziah, who will continue his father’s ways (22:52).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the story of Ahab’s house does not end here (cf. 21:29).
